description: We are tech enthusiasts using AI, data science, and software engineering to tackle environmental challenges. For Space Apps 2026, we're building FireBlindspot—a platform harmonizing NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite data to resolve wildfire detection gaps, uncover historical burn patterns, and deliver clear geospatial insights. We welcome curious, motivated teammates in AI/ML, Python, GIS, full-stack dev, UI/UX, and research. Let's build something impactful together!
summary:
SpectraFuse turns more than two decades of NASA satellite hotspot records into an interactive calendar for exploring when and where burning activity has occurred. It addresses NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS harmonization challenge by putting historical MODIS counts on a common VIIRS scale and showing which values are observed, estimated, or unavailable. Users can explore seasonal patterns, compare sensors, and ask plain-language questions that the AI assistant answers using the underlying data.

An individual grower can check when nearby areas have historically seen more burning before choosing a planting window. The same evidence can support early site screening for agricultural and real estate teams and give geologists and other Earth scientists configurable maps and downloadable data for their own analyses. The prototype covers Sri Lanka comparison area. Its historical calendar supports planning and identifies periods worth monitoring. Future fire forecasting would require additional data and validation.
details:
What we built.

SpectraFuse is a web application with a machine learning model backbone trained using regression for exploring historical burning activity from NASA FIRMS satellite hotspot records. Users can select a region and year, switch between raw and harmonized counts, drill into a month or map area, and export the data as CSV. Seasonal comparisons show how a month differs from earlier years for the same calendar month.

How we harmonized the sensors.

We validated and deduplicated daily MODIS and VIIRS detections and aggregated each sensor’s records into monthly counts when all daily files were present. For earlier months where both sensors had complete records, we divided total VIIRS Suomi-NPP detections by total MODIS detections to fit a regional scaling factor. We reserved the most recent quarter of overlapping months for testing. The calendar uses observed Suomi-NPP counts when available and scales complete MODIS counts when Suomi-NPP is unavailable. It labels each value by source and leaves missing months visible. NOAA-20 provides a separate comparison series.

What we measured.

In the Sri Lanka pilot, scaling reduced mean absolute error on held-out regional monthly totals from about 456 to 138 detections per month, a 70% reduction. Error increased when we applied the same factor to individual grid cells by day. We use the result to support regional monthly comparisons. Hotspot counts describe satellite detections and can include repeat observations or non-fire heat sources.

How the AI assistant works.

The assistant uses a retrieval-augmented workflow. For a question about a region, month, or sensor, it retrieves the relevant NASA FIRMS records from the project’s Parquet archive and uses deterministic Python tools to calculate counts, comparisons, and seasonal departures. It also retrieves project methodology when users ask how an estimate was produced. The assistant explains the results in plain language and can surface the sensor source, coverage and calculation steps, or open the relevant map view. In the live demo, it compared 206 harmonized detections in Sri Lanka in March 2023 with a historical March median of 496.

Who it helps.

A grower can ask which months historically saw more burning near a cultivation area and use that information when planning field checks or choosing a planting window. Companies can use the same workflow for preliminary agricultural and real estate site screening. Geologists and other Earth scientists can select dates, sensor layers and areas of interest, then export the underlying data for further analysis. The prototype combines a Python and FastAPI backend with Parquet storage and a React and Leaflet, Open street dashboard deployed on Vercel.
